Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.

payload.instruction: Stuffing the paper into the cup
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: In the edited image, can the source-image paper and cup be identified, and is that paper visibly stuffed inside that cup?
node.criteria: Pass only if the edited image provides enough visual evidence to identify the same paper and cup shown in the source and shows the paper placed inside the cup with evidence it has been stuffed into it. Fail only if both objects are identifiable and the paper is visibly outside the cup or merely on its rim. Unknown if either object's identity, or their placement, cannot be established.
node.binding: Anchor “the paper” and “the cup” to the objects in the source image. Do not treat a visually different-looking item or object in the edited image as the same object without sufficient evidence.

node_traces.evidence: The source shows a white paper-like item and a blue cup, but the edited image shows a blue printed item and a reddish object. There is not enough visual evidence to identify these as the same paper and cup from the source or establish that the paper was stuffed inside the cup.

fulfillment: The node is already correctly structured to distinguish completion, partial progress, and no progress; the failure is that its evidence path leaves both checks unresolved. Improve the binding/evidence criteria so the checks compare the source and edited images for plausible object continuity despite changes in appearance, while requiring visible evidence of the requested relation. Here, the source has a white sheet and blue cup; the edit shows a hand-held blue printed sheet overlapping a reddish rounded object. Do not assume these are the same objects, but assess whether the sheet is visibly entering or inside the cup, merely near/on its rim, or whether any requested progress is evident. The shown overlap alone does not establish stuffing or identify the reddish object as the cup, so retain uncertainty if that ambiguity cannot be resolved. Avoid treating high confidence in an unresolved judgment as evidence, and do not force the reference label: it constrains the aggregate, not the atomic visual facts. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is indicated; this is an evidence/identity and criterion-resolution issue.
s2: Refine the binding and criteria to make the visual test operational: compare source and edit for plausible continuity of the paper and cup even when viewpoint, color, or appearance changes, then separately assess whether the paper visibly advances toward or into the identified cup. Distinguish paper merely overlapping, touching, or resting near a rim from evidence of entry/placement; overlap alone is not proof of stuffing. In these images, the edit shows a hand-held blue printed sheet overlapping a reddish rounded object, while the source shows white paper and a blue cup. Do not assume either object identity from color or overlap, but explicitly evaluate those cues and the visible relation before deciding. Preserve unknown when identity or progress remains genuinely indeterminate; do not convert uncertainty into “no” to match the aggregate reference. The trace is a valid visual uncertainty, not a transport, schema, or dependency failure. Also avoid treating high confidence in an unresolved result as evidence; improve evidence resolution rather than confidence wording.
